title: The trial of the created Qur'an
word: The trial of the created Qur'an
hookLine: a question of theology becomes a test given by the state, and one scholar won't give the answer

cards: Questions of theology usually live in books and lecture halls. You can disagree about them over dinner and still pass the bread. But for a stretch of the Abbasid caliphate, one question went to court.
Judges and scholars were called in and asked, one by one: is the Qur'an created? There was a right answer, and the government had chosen it. Some said the words and went home.
Some would not, and among them was a scholar in Baghdad, Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

teach.b: The episode has a name in Arabic: al-mihna, the trial, or the ordeal.
It began with the caliph al-Ma'mun, who took up the Mu'tazili view that the Qur'an was created and ordered officials to test the scholars on it.
Those who refused could lose their posts, or worse, and the policy outlived him, carrying on under the caliphs after him. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, whose name the Hanbali school carries, kept refusing.
The accounts of his life, collected by his family and students, say he was held in chains, questioned, and beaten.
And they give his answer again and again, in one shape: show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. They also show what he did not do.
He didn't call for a revolt, raise an army, or curse the caliph from the pulpit. He just wouldn't say the sentence. Some reports say that afterward he forgave the men who had him beaten.

In time a later caliph, al-Mutawakkil, ended the policy. Two things came out of it. In Sunni theology, Ibn Hanbal's position, that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, became the standard one.
And the scholars took a lesson about who settles questions of belief. A ruler had tried, with prisons and whips, and it hadn't worked.
The state stepped in, and the state stepped back out. What stayed was a quiet man who kept asking for a verse.

how: Muslims remember the mihna as the time caliphs tried to enforce the doctrine of the created Qur'an, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal is honored, especially among Sunnis, for refusing under pressure.

games.q: what does “the trial of the created qur'an” mean?
o: a court case over who could print and sell copies of the Qur'an
when caliphs tested scholars on whether the Qur'an was created
a scholars' debate contest held each year in Baghdad's mosques

p: the caliph who began the test
asked for a verse or a sunnah
the caliph who ended the policy

s: Ahmad ibn Hanbal led a revolt against the caliph
the accounts say he refused the sentence but never called for rebellion.
the trial began under the caliph al-Ma'mun

games.q: you're Ahmad ibn Hanbal. officials of the caliph demand you say the Qur'an is created. what do you do?
o: say the words to get free.
denounce the caliph and call for revolt.
refuse calmly, and ask for a proof from the Qur'an or the sunnah.
games.why: the accounts say he kept asking for a verse or a sunnah, bore prison and beating, and never called for rebellion.

practice: Sit up a little straighter, the way you might in a hard meeting, and bring to mind one thing you hold to, something you'd quietly decline to say even if it made life easier.

Notice your jaw and hands, and let the shoulders drop while you keep the conviction: firmness doesn't need clenching. If you pray, ask in your own words for steadiness; if not, just keep the posture, back straight, shoulders soft.

wordCard.voice: The trial of the created Qur'an. Al-mihna: when caliphs enforced the Mu'tazili view, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused to give the answer. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the trial, or ordeal; the name for this episode.

carryVoice: Your line: the state stepped in. And a quiet scholar outlasted it. Until tomorrow.
